narrativeBlocks.title: Two brothers, one throne
narrativeBlocks.body: Oedipus's sons killed each other in civil war: Eteocles defending Thebes, Polynices attacking it. Creon, the new king, honours the defender with full burial — and leaves the attacker's body to rot, a warning to traitors.

narrativeBlocks.title: Antigone's answer
narrativeBlocks.body: Their sister Antigone defies the edict: divine law and family duty outrank a king's decree. She walks out and buries her brother — scattering dust on the corpse herself when the guards undo her work.

narrativeBlocks.title: Creon cannot bend
narrativeBlocks.body: Caught, she does not apologise — she argues. Creon cannot back down without weakening the new throne. So he sentences her to be walled alive in a cave: the state versus the family, neither willing to break first.

narrativeBlocks.title: The cascade
narrativeBlocks.body: Too late, the prophet Tiresias warns Creon that the unburied corpse pollutes the city. Creon relents — but the cave is already empty: Antigone has hanged herself. His son Haemon (her betrothed) kills himself beside her; his mother follows. The 'stable' city loses its ruling family in an afternoon.

narrativeBlocks.title: The argument that never resolves
narrativeBlocks.body: Antigone is the foundational text of conscientious objection — every generation re-fights her case. Sophocles gives both sides real arguments; the tragedy is that both are right.

quiz.prompt: What does Antigone defend in burying Polynices?

choices.text: Divine law and family duty — burial rites owed to the dead, above the king's decree

quiz.explanation: Her argument is with unwritten divine law, not with Creon's politics — which is why the conflict can't be resolved by compromise.

choices.text: Creon relents too late — Antigone is already dead, and his son and wife follow her
The chorus persuades Creon in time

quiz.explanation: The tragedy isn't the wrong choice — it's the delayed right one.
